title: Why 2^{n/2} beats 2^n: the birthday bound
summary: Hash security against collisions is not "try every output." It is the birthday paradox: about square-root many samples already collide with high probability. We compute the bound on a 16-bit toy hash.

case.name: MD5 chosen-prefix collisions (certificates and tooling)
case.impact: Once collision resistance collapsed for MD5, attackers could forge colliding X.509 certificates and break assumptions in tools that still trusted the hash

body:
Pick people uniformly at random and ask when two share a birthday. With 365 days the surprising answer is that probability crosses one half near 23 people — far below 365. The same counting argument rules collision resistance for cryptographic hashes.

Model a hash as a uniform random function to a set of size N = 2^b (b-bit digest). Draw n independent outputs. The number of pairs is n(n−1)/2. Each pair collides with probability about 1/N, so the expected number of colliding pairs is roughly n²/(2N). When that expectation reaches a constant, collisions become likely. Solving n²/(2N) ≈ 1 gives n ≈ √(2N) ≈ 2^{b/2}. A more careful calculation uses
  P(collision) = 1 − exp(−n(n−1)/(2N))
 and asks for the smallest n with P ≥ 1/2, which is about 1.177√N.

That is why a 128-bit hash is often described as having a 64-bit collision security level, and why MD5's collapse mattered operationally: once practical collisions existed, anything that assumed "different inputs ⇒ different MD5" was lying — including certificate public keys in the infamous rogue CA demonstration. SHA-1 later followed a similar path; modern protocols moved to SHA-256 and SHA-3 precisely so that 2^{b/2} stays out of reach.

As an auditor you use the bound in two directions. Designing a commitment or Merkle leaf tag: if an attacker can choose about 2^{b/2} messages, assume they can find a collision unless the hash is unbroken. Reviewing a protocol that truncates a hash to 64 bits "for space": collision work drops to about 2^{32} trials — feasible. The birthday bound is also why you never use a short hash as a unique identifier for untrusted uploads.

ZKCTF's race commitments hash player-visible puzzle data into a binding digest before the round opens. The security claim is preimage / binding strength of that digest, not a truncated toy. Truncation is where birthday math quietly deletes your security margin.

Exercise skill: given N, compute the smallest n with 1 − exp(−n(n−1)/(2N)) ≥ 1/2. You do not need a CAS — try values near 1.177√N and check the formula.

exercise.statement: A toy hash has a 16-bit digest, so N = 65536. Find the smallest integer n such that P(at least one collision among n uniform outputs) ≥ 1/2, using P = 1 − exp(−n(n−1)/(2N)). Answer ZKCTF{n}.
artifacts:
N = 2^16 = 65536
P(n) = 1 - exp(-n*(n-1)/(2*N))
Report the minimal n with P(n) >= 0.5.
hints: Start near 1.177 · √65536 ≈ 301 and test n and n+1 in the formula.
You want the first n where the probability crosses one half; it is a three-digit number.
